chunk-001:c001.proposition: Paul understood Jesus as a physical Jewish man, born under the law and descended from Abraham, whose death, burial, crucifixion, and resurrection concerned an earthly body.

orphanFallback.rationale: Boyce presents Paul's descriptions of birth, Jewish identity, death, burial, crucifixion, and resurrection as affirmative evidence for an earthly Jesus without depending on an opposing move.

chunk-001:c002.proposition: Paul's designation of James as the brother of the Lord identifies a particular biological relative of Jesus rather than merely one member of the Christian community.

orphanFallback.rationale: Boyce independently grounds the biological reading in the identifying function of a relational description attached to the common personal name James.

chunk-001:c004.proposition: Hegesippus preserves a remembered succession of Jesus's physical relatives in Jerusalem leadership extending into the early second century.

orphanFallback.rationale: The cited tradition about Jude's descendants and continuing family leadership stands as affirmative later corroboration of an earthly Jesus with traceable relatives.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-02.proposition: Paul's allegorical discussion in Galatians culminates in the literal event of God sending his son in the fullness of time to be born of a woman.

orphanFallback.rationale: Even without the preserved objection, Boyce's distinction between the surrounding allegory and its claimed literal culmination supplies a positive reading of Paul's birth language.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-04.proposition: Tacitus's specific identification of the time, Roman ruler, and execution context suggests that he traced Christianity's origin through Roman records rather than Christian rumor alone.

orphanFallback.rationale: Boyce's appeal to Tacitus's access and precise chronological and administrative details independently advances an archival-source explanation for the Roman account.

chunk-003:chunk-003-candidate-08.proposition: Although brother terminology can describe a religious group, attaching that description to the common personal name James ordinarily functions as specific identification and supports biological kinship.

orphanFallback.rationale: Boyce concedes generic group usage but affirmatively distinguishes named constructions through parallel ancient practices of adding relational descriptions to disambiguate individuals.

chunk-004:chunk004-candidate-08.proposition: Paul's Pharisaic background, persecution mission, and transformative Damascus experience support his belief that a real executed man underwent bodily resurrection.

orphanFallback.rationale: Boyce presents Paul's persecution and subsequent change concerning what happened to Jesus's body as a self-contained account of conversion centered on an executed person.

chunk-005:c005-01.proposition: Paul presents the five-hundred-witness report as an open contemporary claim that readers could investigate because many of the reported witnesses remained alive.

orphanFallback.rationale: Paul's statement that many witnesses remained alive is used by Boyce as affirmative evidence that the appearance tradition was exposed to contemporary checking.

chunk-006:chunk-006-candidate-002.proposition: Evidence that reported events concerning Jesus occurred would support their historicity without by itself proving every theological claim made about him.

orphanFallback.rationale: Boyce's distinction between corroborating historical occurrences and establishing stronger theological conclusions supplies a standalone evidential standard for interpreting the surviving testimony.

chunk-006:chunk-006-candidate-005.proposition: Pre-Christian interpreters at Qumran used the Davidic covenant to anticipate a future messiah in David's line, showing that the prophecy retained an earthly dynastic expectation.

orphanFallback.rationale: The appeal to pre-Christian Qumran interpretation independently establishes a historical comparative context in which Davidic prophecy generated expectation of a future dynastic messiah.
